name: Enicepatide
lead: Enicepatide (CT-388, RO7795068) is an investigational once-weekly injectable drug that activates the GLP-1 and GIP receptors, developed by Roche for obesity and type 2 diabetes.[1][2] It is described as signal-biased, meaning it shows minimal beta-arrestin coupling at either receptor.[1]

Wikipedia cites a 24-week trial with 18.8 percent placebo-adjusted weight loss.[1] Roche has registered phase 3 trials in people with obesity, with and without type 2 diabetes, including a comparison with tirzepatide.[6][7][8] It is not approved.

paras: Enicepatide is a unimolecular peptide whose cAMP signalling is biased at both GLP-1 and GIP receptors; preclinical models were reported to show greater weight loss with biased agonism than unbiased agonism.[2]

A phase 1 trial enrolled 129 participants, including adults with overweight, obesity and type 2 diabetes.[3] Phase 2 trials enrolled 469 participants with obesity or overweight and a comorbidity and 447 with type 2 diabetes.[4][5] Wikipedia cites press releases reporting over 8 percent weight loss in four weeks in early data and 18.8 percent placebo-adjusted loss at 24 weeks.[1] Phase 3 trials with 2000 participants without type 2 diabetes and 1600 with type 2 diabetes began recruiting in March 2026.[6][7] A planned trial compares it with tirzepatide in type 2 diabetes, a cardiovascular outcomes trial of 8,200 participants is planned, and a phase 2 study will test it with petrelintide.[8][9] The class is reviewed more broadly in an overview of emerging GLP-1 agonists.[10]

quick.overview:
Enicepatide is a weekly injectable that activates GLP-1 and GIP receptors, from Roche. It is in phase 3 for obesity and type 2 diabetes.

Wikipedia cites 18.8 percent placebo-adjusted weight loss at 24 weeks in a trial.
quick.mechanism: A signal-biased dual agonist of GLP-1 and GIP receptors with minimal beta-arrestin coupling.
quick.risks: Investigational and unapproved; published safety information is limited in available sources.
